articles.title_orig: Midterm losses, Nvidia scandal weaken Trump as he faces Xi and Putin
articles.title_zh: Midterm losses, Nvidia scandal weaken Trump as he faces Xi and Putin
articles.content_orig:
China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders.
That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine.
While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025.
"For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors.
Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI.
The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda.
"He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world , whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call . The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.
China has no interest in engaging in nuclear disarmament talks until it achieves parity with the U.S. in about 10 years, said David Roche, strategist at Quantum Strategy.
Putin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.
The summit will likely yield little concrete result, but presents an "almost 100% photo op" that lifts China's status and power at the top table, said Roche, while Trump's political standing slides. Nvidia and the chip-smuggling issues involving a suspected Chinese spy will stay off the agenda, as Trump steers clear of thorny issues where he is unlikely to claim success.
China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election.
China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement.
"Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability."
A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship.
Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP.
U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

articles.title_orig: President Trump travels to Asia for high-stakes summit with China, Russia
articles.title_zh: President Trump travels to Asia for high-stakes summit with China, Russia
articles.content_orig:
Questions remain about the Nvidia CEO's relationship with alleged Chinese spy.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The president's trip comes as questions linger about what the administration knew about prominent tech CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials said they do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will have a bilateral meeting ahead of the trilateral, though Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels. Officials did not specify his reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to Musk's business interests in China.
An official said they expect some additional U.S. business leaders to be attending the APEC CEO Summit, but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump is expected to leave Washington in the morning of Monday, Nov. 16 and arrive in Manila in the evening of Tuesday, Nov. 17, and will head to a bilateral meeting with the other members of the Quad, a diplomatic partnership the U.S. has with Australia, India, and Japan, about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand.
He will then participate in an ASEAN cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
The next day, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony at Malacañang Presidential Palace, the official residence of Filipino President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Romualdez Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. He will also participate in an Association of Southeast Asian Nations cocktail reception followed by a summit dinner.
After Wednesday’s events in the Philippines, Trump travels to Shenzhen, China, where it is expected that a minister will greet Trump on the tarmac. He will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon local time, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Chinese President Xi.
The historic trilateral Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia swing.
Each of Trump and Xi’s meetings this year have been clouded by other topics.
When Trump visited China in May, the raging war in Iran overshadowed the state visit that was scheduled after a detente in Trump's tit-for-tat trade war. Also, when Trump welcomed Xi in September, the pomp and circumstance Trump had planned went without live TV coverage after his banning outlets from the press pool led to a network boycott.
Now, in the background of this trip, is the scandal involving Nvidia's CEO, Huang, who joined Trump's last trip to China earlier this year after boarding Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, according to pool reports at the time. Huang was reported to have had an affair with Alice Huang , a Chinese national and tech executive who is accused of being a Chinese spy.
Officials said they do not expect Trump to raise the allegations against Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, with President Xi, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Huang resigned from Nvidia's board and as its president and CEO on Nov. 12.
This scandal engulfing Huang has introduced scrutiny over Trump’s ties to him and what Trump and other administration officials knew about the relationship with the alleged spy.
"Well, I've been hearing about it and I've been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9.
When pressed on if he was aware of the allegations during his May trip to China, Trump said: "No, I didn't hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had."
On May 12, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the plot. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said.
A U.S. official and a source familiar with the matter told ABC News that after Air Force One landed in China, White House officials asked for business leaders -- including Huang -- to be allowed into a meeting with President Xi. Initially, the Chinese were hesitant to adjust the program, but ultimately agreed to it.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, one of the world’s most-valuable companies and the maker of chips that top AI companies heavily rely on, has been a constant presence around Trump, who has invited tech executives to multiple events, both at the White House and on overseas trips. Since April 28, when Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a state dinner for King Charles III and Queen Camila, the tech CEO has participated in at least six events with Trump, including the September state dinner for Xi.
Huang has lobbied for policy positions that benefit China and Chinese companies over the past few months.
For example, the U.S. has long blocked China's access to American AI chips. However, in December 2025, after lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened those restrictions -- approving the sale of some older but still powerful chips to China as part of a remarkable deal that gave the U.S. government a 25% cut of the sales.
And in July of this year, Huang joined the social media platform X to push back against possible bans on open-weight AI models, the type that Chinese companies have embraced, and which would be cheaper for businesses and governments to adopt. The ban would benefit American companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which use closed models. The U.S. was reportedly considering those bans.
"The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models," Huang wrote in his first-ever X post.
This trip marks Trump's first one overseas since American voters handed him and Republicans a devastating defeat in the midterm elections. Voter Polls show voters rejected the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran -- two of Trump's key foreign policy positions.
The tariffs have been ensnared in legal challenges in count -- and Democrats, who will take the majority in January, have vowed to counter them and reassert congressional authority over trade. They don’t have a veto-proof majority, however, and Trump has vowed to use his veto pen to kill bills he doesn't like.

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Moves to Close A.I. Chip Loophole Ahead of China Trip
articles.content_orig:
Americans are anxious about artificial intelligence . In the midterm elections , they voted to slow down its expansion. Forty local ballot measures in 10 states promise to tighten restrictions on data-center construction, with overwhelming public support. Measures to limit development of data centers won more than 70% of the vote in 30 of these electoral contests. A 2026 survey by Pew Research Center found that about 52% of Americans were more concerned than excited about the growing use of AI in daily life, up from 37% in 2021. Only 9% were more excited than concerned, and roughly six in ten said they wanted more control over how AI is used in their lives.
The sources of anxiety about AI are many: the safety of increasingly powerful systems and the ability to control them; the fear of job displacement; surveillance and the loss of privacy; a rising tide of misinformation and deep fakes; the enormous amounts of electricity and water that the data centers consume; and the concentration of wealth and power in a handful of companies that own the frontier AI models.
Until now, anxiety about the role of AI in geopolitical competition has largely been confined to policy circles. But the possibility that Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday, may have been compromised in a potential espionage scandal has brought that anxiety into the broader public sphere, fueling a frenzy over AI and the competition between the United States and China.
China is at the center of arguably two of the world’s most consequential economic and political developments: its dominance in global trade and its formidable AI capabilities. China and America are AI superpowers, but their strengths differ. America leads in computing power, thanks largely to Nvidia’s advanced chips. China is catching up fast in AI models. The economic and geopolitical implications of this competition are enormous.
There is another dimension to this competition: the economic effects of China’s trade dominance and the rising role of AI in the economy could reinforce each other and produce greater impact than either would have alone. China’s trade dominance is well-known. Two decades earlier, the economists David H. Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon H. Hanson gave that anxiety a name when they coined the term “ China Shock ” to describe the impact of the massive increase in Chinese exports to the U.S. in the early 2000s. The surge contributed to a sharp decline in American manufacturing and the loss of more than two million jobs in certain regions of the United States. Over the past two decades, the so-called China Shock has gone global, as Chinese exports have surged around the world without a comparable rise in China’s imports.
The world may soon experience the convergence of two enormous economic shocks, each reinforcing the other in terms of their direction and magnitude: The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock. The consequences of AI-driven productivity growth remain contested. But the fear is that AI will enable companies to dramatically increase output without employing more people or raising the income of ordinary citizens. The China Shock has a similar effect. China has become a dominant force in advanced manufacturing in electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, artificial intelligence, and robotic technology. But China’s growing competitiveness has led to a global surge of Chinese exports without a corresponding global surge of Chinese imports.
On top of the China Shock, the AI Productivity Shock could further widen the gap between global supply and demand, and create new economic imbalances and strains on a scale the world has not witnessed.
The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock share one critical feature: both can produce a glut of output without generating a corresponding increase in demand. In China, production has grown faster than consumption; with AI, the fear is that the technology will generate wealth without creating jobs. In both cases, the gains tend to flow to the owners of capital—and in China’s case, also to the government—rather than to workers and households.
But the iron law of economics still holds: supply requires demand, and an economy can absorb a large increase in output only if enough people have the income to buy what it produces. Economists have long described it as a problem of effective demand: the recognition that supply does not automatically create its own demand. For that to happen, greater production and supply have to translate into more jobs and higher incomes.
Whether AI will create such an imbalance is still a matter of debate. Optimists point to earlier waves of automation. Technologies such as the tractor and the spreadsheet displaced certain kinds of work but eventually helped create other kinds of work and generated jobs and additional income for workers. Only time will tell whether AI, which differs significantly from earlier technologies, will follow that pattern. What we do know is that this optimistic scenario of technological progress has yet to deliver the gains in employment and household purchasing power in China.
China is now regarded as one of the world’s leading technological powers. In some industries, China’s factories are producing more than the global demand put together. China makes more than 80% of the world’s solar panels, and its factories can turn out roughly twice as many modules in a year as the entire planet installs. In batteries, China’s manufacturing capacity is already more than double the current global demand. One projection suggests that, by 2030, China alone could produce more batteries than the whole world will use.
But China’s technological advancement is far more visible in what its factories can produce than in what its households can afford to buy and consume. Youth unemployment in the country is rising, and domestic consumption has stagnated. The unemployment rate among urban Chinese aged 16 to 24 climbed to a record 18.9 % in August 2025, according to official statistics. The real figure is likely to be much higher.
Economic progress is defined by progress in both production and consumption. These two areas of human activity move in tandem with each other and are mutually reinforcing. Faster productivity leads to rising output , which raises incomes and allows households to buy more of what is being produced. Historically, before the age of AI, this has been the case. The China Shock and the AI Productivity Shock may break that connection. What made, and continues to make, the China Shock so disruptive is the immense disparity between the scale of China’s exports and its purchases from the rest of the world. China’s imports consist largely of agricultural products, minerals, and energy products that it cannot produce in sufficient quantities on its soil.
China’s exports lower prices for consumers abroad, a benefit on the expenditure side. But households need income to consume, and that income comes from the production side of the economy. But the Chinese economy is not generating a corresponding increase in income for the rest of the world by importing more from them and boosting their production. China has roughly 35% of the world’s manufacturing capacity but accounts for about just 11% of global consumption. Household consumption in the country amounts to a mere 39% of its GDP, compared with 68% in America. This imbalance is unsustainable—for both China and the world.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on third-country loophole that allowed China to use computing power
articles.title_zh: Nvidia fallout: Commerce cracks down on third-country loophole that allowed China to use computing power
articles.content_orig:
The Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing export controls on sensitive technology.
Commerce's action, an interim final rule issued by its Bureau of Industry and Security, is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week.
The department said in a press release that the rule was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council."
The rule came after rising criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been accused of not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls.
"The Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests," the IFR says.
"These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models," the rule said.
The rule also says that a license will now "required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in an interview on Friday with CNBC's "Squawk Box," blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company at the center the Nvidia scandal, on the so-called entity list, which would restrict certain exports to it.

articles.title_orig: Scores of Bahraini Shi'ite clerics get life in jail, accused of plotting with Iran
articles.title_zh: Scores of Bahraini Shi'ite clerics get life in jail, accused of plotting with Iran
articles.content_orig:
TEHRAN, Nov. 16 (MNA) – Bahrain's highest religious authority Grand Ayatollah Sheikh Isa Qassim has been sentenced to life imprisonment in Bahrain on Monday.
Bahrain’s High Criminal Court issued a life sentence on Monday, in absentia, against Ayatollah Sheikh Isa Qassim, a prominent Bahraini cleric.
The court session took place following a 40-day conflict, amidst a wave of widespread arrests of religious scholars and activists, as well as the revocation of the citizenship of hundreds of individuals.
Four other clerics have also been sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Prior to this, the Bahraini opposition had dismissed the trial of several prominent Shia clerics, holding the government responsible for the consequences of any convictions that might be handed down against the detained clerics. These groups warned that continuation of such actions would push political crisis into a phase of confrontation that threatens the very existence of one of the core components of Bahraini society.
Opposition forces have called on the people of Bahrain to follow developments and to remain prepared to defend the religious scholars and Shia community, in accordance with the guidance of Ayatollah Sheikh Isa Ahmed Qassim, who has emphasized the importance of remaining loyal to the scholars.

articles.title_orig: Russell Brand prison message denying rape 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
articles.title_zh: Russell Brand prison message denying rape 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
articles.content_orig:
A message by Russell Brand to his followers in which he claimed innocence for his sexual offences was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated, Downing Street has said.
The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules, while Victims' Commissioner for London Andrea Simon said the claims will "certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it".
In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can seen sitting on a sofa and is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.
Relaying the message from her husband, Laura Brand said the comedian - who is currently being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire - called prison staff "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".
She said she had been speaking to him and he "is OK and is praying".
Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.
Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.
"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."
Speaking earlier, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments."
"No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments," he added.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Victim's Commisioner for London Simon added: "The victims during the sentencing hearing highlighted how his denials and ongoing media fame over two decades had added to their pain and trauma," she said.
"The fact survivors are still having to hear this now is really problematic and very concerning that we can't do more to protect them from it."
While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders such as Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".
She added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.
Over the weekend, Brand was moved from the category B HMP Wandsworth in south London to the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a prison that mostly houses sex offenders and has tailored programmes for them.
Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty, told LBC he agreed it was not "a good look" that he'd been moved to a lower security prison.
"I think people want to see him facing the appropriate punishment for what are appalling crimes against women and others and I think the whole episode is shocking," he said.
Meanwhile, there have been calls for a change in the law following Brand's conviction so that sexual relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal. The government says a discussion is to take place.
Mia Latter, who has alleged she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16, is among those campaigning for ministers to introduce a staggered age of consent.
She was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. Brand denied the allegations at the time. None of the women were complainants in his recent criminal trial.
Latter, who was known under the pseudonym "Alice" in the 2023 investigation, has now waived her right to anonymity.
In an interview with LBC on Monday, Latter said: "We don't want to criminalise anybody under the age of 18 [including] 16, 17-year-olds, 18-year-olds having sex with each other...
"I think healthy relationships are important, and they're important in helping you develop and grow."
But she said there should be an age "threshold" for the partners of 16 and 17 year-olds.
Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, is urging a change in the law to prevent 16 year-olds from having a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and someone aged 17 from having a relationship with anyone older than 20.
She told BBC Breakfast that "predators know exactly what they are doing".
Asked about the issue on BBC Breakfast, the foreign secretary said: "I think the reason why it's right to have this debate is we've seen some of the very, very brave victims of Russell Brand come forward and say 'we think this needs looking at'."
Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said she is glad there is a conversation around staggering the age of consent but warned that it had "been quite complicated to actually implement" in some US states where it is used.
Trott said a suggestion that the age of consent should be raised to 18 is also a "conversation we need to have" but "probably isn't practical".
Anna Edmundson, director of policy & social change at the NSPCC charity, said: "We urgently need a review of what is and isn't working to ensure 16 and 17-year-olds are fully protected in law from this predatory behaviour.
"However, closing these gaps will only be part of the solution. We must question why adults have been able to exploit teenagers in plain sight for so long, and look at what further action is needed to help people recognise the signs of exploitation."
Any change in the law would only affect England and Wales as Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate legislative powers in relation to the age of consent, which is also currently set at 16 in both nations.
The Scottish Government said it had "no current plans" to change the age of consent, following the calls by campaigners, but any proposals would be considered.
The foreign secretary also apologised for having appeared on Russell Brand's online show in 2015, when he was Labour leader.
Miliband told Today if he'd known about the allegations then, he would not have done spoken to him, adding: "I deeply regret doing that interview and all my sympathies are with those victims."

articles.title_orig: ‘Two dictators in my story – Duterte and Zuckerberg’: Nobel peace prize winner’s warning for democracy
articles.title_zh: ‘Two dictators in my story – Duterte and Zuckerberg’: Nobel peace prize winner’s warning for democracy
articles.content_orig:
Filipino-US journalist Maria Ressa’s new book is a cri de coeur against the twin threats of authoritarianism and tech oligarchy – and how we can fight back
Maria Ressa keeps apologising. “Sorry, I’m hyper, too much coffee!” she says at one point. “Sorry, I can rant for a long time, so you have to stop me!” she says at another.
Ressa can be forgiven for firing on all cylinders. The Nobel peace prize laureate has just been to a screening in Britain of The Social Reckoning, which offers an unflattering portrayal of the tech titan Mark Zuckerberg, a man she regards as a “dictator”. Now she is speaking to the Guardian at a hotel in Washington’s Dupont Circle a few days before Americans vote in critical midterm elections.
Ressa, a 63-year-old, 5ft 2in force of nature, reflects: “I feel like the train is coming at us in slow motion and we’re standing on the train tracks.”
The Filipino and American journalist has been sounding alarms for a decade . In 2016 she warned Zuckerberg and other Silicon Valley executives that an authoritarian disinformation model being tested in the Philippines would soon be exported to the west. Like Cassandra, she was not believed. Now, with Donald Trump in the White House and tech billionaires actively reshaping the US state, Ressa has a new cri de cœur.
The Fight Back : A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators is a survival manual for confronting the convergence of authoritarian governance and tech oligarchy. It finds democracies facing a crisis of truth (the breakdown of facts and shared reality), a crisis of order (the breakdown of law and international rules) and a crisis of accountability (institutions are captured, the law is weaponised and the most powerful economic and tech actors operate without democratic oversight).
Ressa’s warnings are rooted in experience. She spent nearly two decades as an investigative reporter and bureau chief for CNN in Manila and Jakarta, covering terrorism, ethnic conflict and the precarious transitions of post-authoritarian societies across south-east Asia.
In 2012, convinced that digital technology offered a tool to empower citizens and demand transparency, she co-founded Rappler , an independent, digital-first news organisation in the Philippines. Blending hard-nosed investigative journalism with data science and community engagement, Rappler quickly established itself as a vital watchdog in a fragile democracy.
When Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 , Ressa found herself at the front line of a terrifying global experiment. As Duterte unleashed a bloody extrajudicial drug war that claimed thousands of lives, his regime weaponised social media to silence critics, deploying state-backed troll armies to poison public discourse and wage psychological warfare.
Rappler’s reporting exposed the machinery of manufactured outrage, making Ressa the authoritarian government’s public enemy number one. She endured an onslaught of online harassment, including rape threats and death threats, and an aggressive legal offensive by the state, with 11 cases filed against her, including charges of cyber libel and tax evasion.
Rather than flee or capitulate, she posted bail 10 times and turned her courtroom battles into an international campaign for press freedom. In 2021 she was awarded the Nobel peace prize , alongside Russian journalist Dmitry Muratov, for safeguarding the freedom of expression that underpins democracy.
The personal toll has been immense. “I wish I could get more sleep,” she says matter-of-factly. “I worked in war zones and the only difference is you’d walk into conflict and stay two weeks to a month and then you could come out and decompress for a month. This is a decade of non-decompression.”
Ressa’s experience in the Philippines informs The Fight Back, but she argues that the threat is now much wider. A report published earlier this year by the V-Dem Institute, a Swedish research centre that measures the health of democracies worldwide, found that democracy had fallen back to 1978 levels for the average global citizen, with three-quarters of the world’s population living under autocratic rule.
In the US, the level of democracy had fallen to its lowest point since 1965. The report contained a sentence that Ressa had to read three times and still haunts her: “The speed with which American democracy is currently dismantled is unprecedented in modern history.”
Early in Trump’s second term, comparisons with authoritarian leaders such as Duterte in the Philippines and Viktor Orbán in Hungary were commonplace. But it soon became apparent that the US president was moving with a scope and speed that would leave even those autocrats envious.
Ressa writes: “What took Hungary’s Orbán four years, Serbia’s Vučić eight years, India’s Modi and Turkey’s Erdoğan a decade, Trump accomplished in one year. Legislative constraints lost one-third of their value in 2025, the lowest in more than one hundred years. As in the Philippines, Congress has effectively abdicated its oversight role. At least 55% of the 320 objectives set out by the far-­right Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 have already been achieved.”
The rise of technology has become a driving force behind democratic decay. Ressa writes: “There are two dictators in my story: Duterte and Zuckerberg. This is not hyperbole. This is a statement about power, accountability – and impunity – in the 21st century.”
The fusion of state power and oligarchy was symbolised on 20 January 2025, inauguration day , when tech leaders including Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai, Sergey Brin, Tim Cook and Sam Altman were given prominent seats ahead of Trump’s cabinet nominees as he took the oath of office.
The symbiotic relationship operates through mutual self-interest: autocrats require tech platforms to distribute propaganda and paralyse public opposition, while tech oligarchs require state deregulation, tax relief, military contracts, and protection from international antitrust enforcement.
Which poses the bigger threat, Trump or big tech? Ressa has no hesitation in answering: “The big tech, because they themselves, the CEOs, are now saying: stop us. That’s kind of performative. You can stop yourself! You’re the one building this.”
Even Rappler was built as a digital-first newsroom that partnered with platforms and engineered tech. Wielding her phone, Ressa acknowledges: “We’re frenemies. I like tech. Rappler is a partner of every tech company. We build tech.”
But when she begged tech companies to “prioritise facts”, she realised facts have never been part of the AI equation. “It’s a probabilistic machine, which actually discounts facts. When you put that as the operating system of public information you create what we’re living through now. Then they made it worse because they added algorithms that will keep you scrolling longer so that means fear, anger, hate. It is the worst of who we are.”
She regards big tech as predatory and extractive. Their monopolies built valuations by ingesting journalism without compensation. “The raw material is the world’s knowledge. It is what we write that is expensive. They just scrape it.”
And by engineering algorithms for sensationalism and “outrage machine”, platforms altered human psychology, Ressa argues. “The incentive structure of our world changed with big tech. I always say to my friends who have kids: imagine if you keep telling your child, ‘Lie. I’m going to keep rewarding you, and then keep lying and I’m going to keep rewarding you.’ What kind of adult does your child become? That’s the world we’re creating.”
The new generation of tech overlords are, in her view, dictators. “They make decisions for us without our inputs, without any accountability, and it impacts all of us. This is a public safety issue. It’s like taking the lead out of your water. Every day that governments do not regulate, they lose more and more of their power.”
No figure illustrates this surrender more starkly than Elon

articles.title_orig: Stock futures slide as Nvidia leads AI stocks lower: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures slide as Nvidia leads AI stocks lower: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures fell on Monday, dragged down by key technology stocks, as traders awaited a highly anticipated earnings report from Nvidia and a potentially record-setting public market debut of Anthropic this week.
Nasdaq-100 futures declined 1.4%, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.6%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures shed 90 points, or 0.2%.
Shares in Nvidia were down about 4% in premarket trading. On Monday, the Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese firms rent the chipmaker's computing power located in other countries. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the weekend called for a " dramatic shakeup " at Nvidia, urging its board to look outside the company for its next CEO.
The embattled chipmaker is preparing to report its third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. While analysts expect the company to post nearly 100% year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, investors will be more focused on how the company will move forward after Jensen Huang's exit as chief executive.
Huang last week resigned from his post after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares dropped 13%, marking their biggest weekly slide since April 2025.
"The main task at hand for interim CEO Colette Kress [is to] restore order and give the Street confidence in the Nvidia story going forward," wrote Dan Ives, analyst at Yorkville Ives. "This starts with earnings and the conference call this week on Tuesday after the bell…we still expect guidance and a typical conference call around robust business metrics with demand metrics that have clearly accelerated since last quarter."
Other stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade were under pressure along with Nvidia. Fellow chipmakers Micron Technology , Intel and Advanced Micro Devices each lost more than 5%. Additionally, shares of computer maker Dell Technologies also declined more than 5%, while software stock Oracle moved down nearly 4%.
Another key test for the trade this week is Anthropic's initial public offering. The AI giant is eyeing a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation, with shares expected to be priced between $70 and $78.
Wall Street is coming off a winning week despite Nvidia's tumble. The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted their biggest weekly gains since August, rising more than 2% each.
In Asia, markets closed mostly lower Monday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 dropping 2.42% after third-quarter GDP unexpectedly shrank. South Korea's Kospi slumped 3.59%, leading losses in the region. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.41%. Mainland China's CSI 300 fell 0.91% after downbeat key economic data, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index gained 0.49%.
In Europe, the pan-European Stoxx 600 was up 0.12%. The U.K. FTSE 100 rose 0.28%, while France's CAC 40 advanced 0.30%. Germany's DAX was just above the flatline.
The Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's computing power from locations in other countries.
Commerce's action, in the form of an interim final rule issued by its Bureau of Industry and Security, is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal at Nvidia that led CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week.
The department said in a press release that the rule was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council." Read more .
Factory activity eased in  New York State during November though employment expanded at the fastest pace in more than four years, the regional Federal Reserve reported Monday.
The New York Fed's Empire State Manufacturing Index posted a reading of 7.8, down 18 points from October and below the Dow Jones consensus for 16.7. The index measures the difference between companies reporting growth against contraction, so a positive number still represents expansion.
Much of the decline came in new orders, which fell 20.2 points to 3.0. However, the employment index jumped to 18.1, growth of 7.8 points and its highest since June 2022. Prices also continued to climb but at a slower pace as the prices paid index fell 14 points to 45.9.
Nvidia continues to lose its luster, with two more Wall Street analysts lowering their price targets on the stock following a scandal that led to Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO.
Mizuho, which has an outperform on the chipmaker, lowered its price target on shares to $220 from $250. That still suggests 35% upside from Friday's close. UBS has a buy rating on the stock. It revised its price target on shares down to $240 from $300, which is 47% above the level at which Nvidia last closed.
"We believe ex-CEO Jensen was viewed as the global dealmaker 'AI banker', and key innovator," Mizuho analyst Vijay Rakesh said in a note to clients. "The significant NVDA ~32% stock decline from the Oct peak (vs. the SOX down 23%), reflects the 'Jensen/founder' premium lost. We believe the CEO departure also adds a 6-7-month management overhang, as [the] company comes under the US gov't microscope."
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Check out CNBC's live blog here for more on the stocks making premarket moves.
— Ananya Chetia and Fred Imbert
UniCredit 's takeover of Commerzbank has been given the go-ahead by European competition regulators.
The European Commission on Monday gave antitrust approval to the Italian lender's bid to take control of its German peer, following similar consent from the European Central Bank last month.
That now clears the path for the takeover, with UniCredit's integration plan expected to begin early next year.
"Our approval of UniCredit's acquisition of Commerzbank shows that it is possible to support a stronger European banking sector while safeguarding competition and choice," said Teresa Ribera, the Commission's first executive vice-president for a clean, just and competitive transition.
Shares in Milan-listed UniCredit were 0.62% lower in morning trade. Commerzbank was down 1% in Frankfurt.
Nvidia 's stock fell 1.72% in premarket trading, continuing its slide after losing hundreds of billions in market cap last week amid the fallout from Jensen Huang resigning as CEO.
Nvidia announced Huang was stepping down as CEO on Thursday, amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a spy for China. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday.
Oil prices moved higher on Monday, with Brent crude — the global price benchmark — rising 0.30% to $96.13 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures added 0.49% to $89.03.
The rise comes after two oil tankers reportedly struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters, which cited Iran's Revolutionary Guard. It followed similar reported incidents on Sunday and Monday.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was almost 0.1% higher in early dealmaking, as most continental sectors made gains and major bourses were mixed shortly after 8:10 a.m. in London (3:10 a.m. E.T.).
Healthcare stocks advanced 0.79%, followed by telecommunications, which were up 0.67%, as household goods gained 0.63%. Basic resources shed 1.67%
Among regional bourses, the French CAC 40 led early gains, rising 0.30%, while the U.K. FTSE 100 added 0.22%. Germany's DAX fell 0.10%, and the Italian FTSE MIB was 0.39% down.
European stock markets are expected to start the new trading week in mostly negative territory.
Stoxx 50 futures seen opening almost 0.1% lower, with all of the continent's major bourses in the red.
The French CAC 40 was almost 0.2% down ahead of Monday's session, while the Italian FTSE MIB was about 0.1% lower.
Futures tied to the U.K. FTSE 100 and Germany's DAX were seen opening around the flatline.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine
Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.
A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea , Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.
In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.
Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin.
The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.
after newsletter promotion
Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.
Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.
Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title_orig: Nintendo Store App Receives A Small But Worthwhile Update, Here Are The Patch Notes
articles.title_zh: Nintendo Store App Receives A Small But Worthwhile Update, Here Are The Patch Notes
articles.content_orig:
Remember the dedicated Nintendo Store mobile app? Honestly, we sometimes forget about it too. But hey, Nintendo is still updating it, and the latest patch should make it a little easier to see what you have been up to on your Switch this year.
The ver. 3.4.0 update launched on iOS and Android earlier today, and it seems to be all about making the user experience that bit better.
The big change this time around is that you can now find information about your DLC and other software habits on the Play Activity screen, but there have also been some tweaks to the User Page and more.
Far from anything groundbreaking, then, but a worthwhile little addition to anyone wanting some more info from their Play Activity rundown.
You'll find the (admittedly, very short) patch notes from the App Store below:
・ Information about downloadable content and other types of software can now be found on the play activity screen. ・ Design changes have been made to improve the readability of the user page. ・ Various improvements and fixes have been made.
Do we wish that all of these disparate Nintendo apps were combined into one? Sure! Are we pleased to see Nintendo is still working to improve them behind the scenes? Absolutely.

articles.title_orig: Pope Endures Grueling Travel in South America Weeks After Surgery
articles.title_zh: Pope Endures Grueling Travel in South America Weeks After Surgery
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV wraps up a 12-day homecoming tour of South America on Monday that eased doubts about his recovery from cancer surgery and highlighted the social justice priorities shaping his early papacy.
The 71-year-old pontiff traveled through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru -- a demanding itinerary many doubted he could complete a month after lung surgery.
From the high Andes to the sweltering Amazon, US-born Leo crisscrossed a continent where he spent nearly two decades as a missionary, and picked up Peruvian citizenship along the way.
Visiting care homes and prisons, the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics delivered hard-hitting speeches and browbeat political leaders like Argentina's Javier Milei, insisting growth must benefit all, and speaking in defense of the poor, the elderly and disabled people.
Pulling it off has proved Leo's "incredible strength and determination," which people had largely "underestimated," said Vatican expert Elise Ann Allen, who has written a biography of Chicago-born Leo.
"We're also seeing the missionary pope in a way that we've never seen him before," she told AFP.
In wealthy, secular Uruguay, the pontiff ventured into the most dangerous neighborhood in the capital Montevideo to highlight the deaths of children caught up in drug violence.
He urged greater solidarity with the lonely and suffering, describing the country's high suicide rates as "painful" and demanding greater respect for women, a theme that would return throughout his trip.
In Argentina, Leo drew more than two million people to masses in both Buenos Aires and nearby Lujan -- the biggest of his papacy to date.
He was welcomed by weeping Argentine pilgrims who had long waited in vain for his predecessor, Francis, to return.
Leo visited the notorious Devoto prison, telling inmates there was hope for even the most evil, and told a home for people with disabilities that a nation's progress should be judged by how it treats its most vulnerable citizens.
His likeness appeared on alfajores pastries and jars of dulce de leche as Argentines celebrated the landmark visit.
But it was his return to Peru, and the areas he served as Bishop Robert Francis Prevost, that was the emotional highlight of the trip for Leo.
Three million people lined the streets to welcome him in Lima.
He told them they had formed him as a pastor, saying: "Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you."
From the baking desert to the Andes, crowds chanted "The pope is Peruvian," and old friends welcomed him home.
He met six victims of clerical abuse in Argentina and Peru, including some linked to the once-powerful and now-disbanded Catholic society, Sodalitium Christianae Vitae.
In Peru, he spoke of the "pain" caused by Catholic clerical abuse and said the Church must make "amends" to victims and foster "a culture of prevention and protection."
- River deep, mountain high -
The most physically taxing part of the trip took him from the desert to high-altitude Cusco, the heartland of the Inca Empire, and then down to the hot and humid Amazon basin.
In Pucallpa, he said environmental destruction was threatening both the rainforest and the people who depend on it, and denounced the unacceptable neglect suffered by many Indigenous communities.
"The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable," he said. "The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice."
On Monday, he will visit a center for elderly people and hold a final mass in Lima, before returning to the Vatican.
The pope's cancer diagnosis fewer than 18 months into his papacy shook the Catholic Church, and this trip -- one of the most grueling in decades -- has been closely watched as a barometer of how his papacy may be affected.
As if in response to doubters, Leo said neither old age nor ill health could "extinguish" his religious zeal.
Returning to Latin America has allowed him to "get back in touch with the roots of who he is," biographer Allen said. "I think it's going to awaken something in him."
"I think we're seeing a new chapter of Pope Leo's papacy begin," she said.

articles.title_orig: Chip tensions loom over Trump-Xi summit, as US and China push AI safety steps
articles.title_zh: Chip tensions loom over Trump-Xi summit, as US and China push AI safety steps
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock falls as Jensen Huang reportedly weighs CEO comeback, Musk backs return
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock falls as Jensen Huang reportedly weighs CEO comeback, Musk backs return
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock futures fell 3% on Monday as investors digested a report that supporters of Jensen Huang are lobbying for his return to the AI chip giant following his abrupt resignation last week.
Huang has discussed returning as CEO with confidants, the Financial Times reported Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. Huang resigned last week following reports of affairs, including one with a woman who was reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.
According to the report, a Huang supporter said that a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being assembled to lobby Nvidia's board to reinstate him, including by seeking support from the White House.
"Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the person said, adding that Huang supported the effort.
Meanwhile, SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) CEO Elon Musk has come out in support of Huang, writing on X last Friday , "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I'm signing it too."
On Saturday, Musk said , "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract. Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
The push to bring Huang back comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached Arm Holdings ( ARM ) CEO Rene Haas as it searches for a successor. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO during the search.
Yorkville's Dan Ives said that while "no one individual can replace Jensen as CEO," any talk of "Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/Board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles."
Huang abruptly stepped down Thursday following reports of alleged affairs with a former executive from Singapore-based Megaspeed, and also an Nvidia employee who reported directly to him.
Days earlier, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife but did not disclose how many affairs he had or identify those involved.
Recent reports have raised concerns about whether restricted semiconductors were being diverted to China and if sensitive US information had been sent to Beijing.
The developments have also sent shockwaves through the AI industry, where Nvidia has played a central role in building the ecosystem. The company has become a bellwether for the AI trade and has invested in key parts of the industry, including large language model development, energy, optics, and cloud providers.
Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results Tuesday after the bell, in what will be the company's first earnings call without Huang.
The stock declined more than 12% last week, closing below a $4 trillion market cap. At least 10 Wall Street analysts have recently downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold, with many citing, in part, increased scrutiny in Washington and succession uncertainty.

articles.title_orig: Prince Harry salutes wounded Ukrainian veterans as ‘role models’ on surprise Ukraine visit
articles.title_zh: Prince Harry salutes wounded Ukrainian veterans as ‘role models’ on surprise Ukraine visit
articles.content_orig:
The Duke of Sussex has received an enthusiastic welcome in a surprise visit to Ukraine to support injured war veterans, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.
There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women in Lviv, where he told his audience: "You're going to win the war."
Prince Harry spent two days at events for veterans, with a press blackout for security reasons until he had left Ukraine, as the country continues to face missile attacks from Russia.
Ukraine has more than 150,000 injured war veterans and the prince visited projects supporting their treatment and rehabilitation.
"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," he said - with technology advancing in areas such as drone warfare, but also in protecting cities and providing treatment.
A mobile phone app is where Ukrainians look for air raid warnings, telling them the direction, timing and type of any incoming missiles.
At the Superhumans Center near Lviv, Harry was shown how growing numbers of injured veterans receive groundbreaking treatment.
International experts used to come to help Ukraine, he said, but "now that has flipped," with Ukraine having the greater expertise with trauma injuries to share with others.
That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.
In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.
He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".
"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.
"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.
At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.
He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.
In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.
And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."
Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.
Olga Rudeva, chief executive of the SuperHumans Center, said it is seeing more injured civilians than ever because of "changes to the frontlines".
"The Russians are doing double taps , they are targeting civilian infrastructure," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
As a result, "it's not only about [an] increased number of patients, it's about increased complexity of new cases."
Russia has repeatedly denied it aims for civilian targets.
At a noisy sports centre in Lviv, Prince Harry arrived to watch a wheelchair rugby match taking place, with some thunderous collisions between the players.
He was welcomed by the competitors in what he has called his Invictus "family" and soon the visit turned into something approaching a group hug, with Harry disappearing into a sea of selfies and handshakes.
He was presented with a T-shirt remembering prisoners of war held by Russian forces.
And he later had a chance to play one of the events at the Invictus Games, a tennis-style competition called pickleball.
Watching was Ivan Voinov, who has lost a leg and suffered head injuries, but who is using sport to help his rehabilitation - including learning to dance again.
He said that dancing was his way to be together with his wife again, which meant so much to his recovery and recovering his identity.
At an Invictus awards ceremony during the visit, Prince Harry was greeted with choruses of "Harry, Harry, Harry", getting a rock star welcome.
"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.
He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".
There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.
The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.
Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.
"These people have so much to offer," he said.
"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

articles.title_orig: China stands with the people of the Middle East and Africa, on right side of history: Foreign Ministry
articles.title_zh: China stands with the people of the Middle East and Africa, on right side of history: Foreign Ministry
articles.content_orig:
Restrictions have affected Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones
A crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly and affecting Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said.
The issue over the speed of the Starshield system - a military-grade service developed by Elon Musk's Starlink and provided to Ukraine by the US government - has been rumbling on for weeks.
Zelensky said he had asked officials "to work as closely as possible" with the US government and Musk's company. "It is important to be on the right side of history," he said. The BBC has asked the White House and Starlink for comment.
US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.
On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".
"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.
"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try to carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

articles.title_orig: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
articles.title_zh: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion, says kindness 'compounds' in Thanksgiving letter
articles.content_orig:
Billionaire Warren Buffett donated Berkshire Hathaway shares worth about $5.5 billion to four philanthropic foundations, stepping up his annual charitable giving from the prior year.
Buffett, 96, converted 6,150 Class A Berkshire shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares and gave 3,690,000 of those shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, and 1,845,000 shares to each of The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and NoVo Foundation — the foundations run by his three children, Susie, Howard and Peter Buffett.
Following the donations, the chairman emeritus of Berkshire still owns 182,140 Class A shares — roughly $162 billion.
"Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie and I ever bought," wrote Buffett, who was succeeded as chairman in September by his son Howard, in his annual Thanksgiving message.
The letter was much shorter than his message last Thanksgiving. Charlie Munger, former vice chairman of Berkshire, passed away in November 2023.
Berkshire shares have been on a tear recently, up more than 19% since the start of the fourth quarter and ending last week with four consecutive record high closes. That compares with the S&P 500's decline of 1.2% so far for the fourth quarter. Berkshire has been seen as a safe haven as investors have worried about the AI buildout, corporate drama and geopolitical risk.
The shares are now outperforming the S&P 500 for the year by about 7.5 percentage points.
In his letter, Buffett reiterated that all of his Berkshire shares eventually will be donated to the four foundations, with the goal being to increase the size of the grants each year.
Buffett wrote that the gifts were a signal of his confidence not only in his three children, but also in Berkshire CEO Greg Abel:
"My children have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity...You heard plenty from me in September about my confidence in Berkshire. That confidence is as strong as ever," he said.
Referring to Munger and himself, Buffett added, "Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received."
"Warren continues to share his wisdom with us all during this holiday season. His example reflects the kindness he encourages in all of us," said CEO Abel of the letter.
Buffett closes his message with this advice: "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."
